description_full: Otis Worldwide Corporation engages in manufacturing, installation, and servicing of elevators and escalators in the United States, China, and internationally. The company operates in two segments, New Equipment and Service. The New Equipment segment designs, manufactures, sells, and installs a range of passenger and freight elevators, as well as escalators and moving walkways for residential and commercial buildings, and infrastructure projects. This segment serves real-estate and building developers, and general contractors. It sells its products directly to customers, as well as through agents and distributors. The Service segment performs maintenance and repair services, as well as modernization services to upgrade elevators and escalators. Otis Worldwide Corporation was founded in 1853 and is headquartered in Farmington, Connecticut.

financial_summary: Otis Worldwide Corporation is a large-cap industrials business with a $29.5B market cap on $14.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 126% against a 8% cost of capital — a 118-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $1.4B in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.15× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.0× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 9.8×.

Shareholder yield of 4.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 6pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.33x).
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-6.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 24% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 6% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 23% and a beta of 0.75, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $295.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 12% in the 2020 crash and 26% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades only 2% below its DCF fair value of $79.36, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 8%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $60.74 to $107 (P10-P90).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-6%).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $86.23 on average, 11% above the price.
The price implies 5.2% annual cash-flow growth.
prof: ROIC of 126% clears the cost of capital of 7.5% by 118pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.47).
It converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.15x.
It spends 1.1% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 3.0x net debt to EBITDA ($1.1B of cash against $8.0B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 9.8x.
The current ratio of 0.85 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.8% over 3 years and 2.5% over 5 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 2.2% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.10 (orders outpacing sales) and a backlog worth 1.3x annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 1.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 99%.
It returns 4.9% a year to shareholders (2.7% in buybacks and 2.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 72,000 employees, each generates about $200K of revenue, 0.6x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 2.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $20K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.8M (19x revenue per employee).
